title: Data Structures and Data Processing in Kasa
description: Five guided, text-first lessons on nested lists, positional records, data validation, aggregates and filtered summaries using only supported core Kasa. Tables and typed records remain concepts or experimental host-side prototypes, not native Kasa builtins.

units.title: Organize rows with nested lists
units.goal: Read two-dimensional list data by row and column positions.
units.concept: A nested list stores one list inside another. Each row here has exactly two numeric entries, and index 0 selects the first column. This is a teaching representation, not a native Kasa table type.
units.source:
ma rows = [[12, 8], [10, 6], [7, 5]]
ma i = 0
bere_a i < tentɛn(rows)
    ma total = rows[i][0] + rows[i][1]
    ka total
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
trace: Start with a list containing three rows, each with two numbers.
At row index 0, add 12 and 8, then print 20.
Repeat for rows 1 and 2 to print 16 and 12; the loop stops at index 3.
units.task: Add a fourth row [6, 4] and predict the extra output. Explain why a missing column would make positional indexing unsafe.
acceptance: Produces correct sums for each row.
Identifies row and column indices correctly.
Explains the two-column assumption and bounds risks.
units.question: What is rows[1][0] in this dataset?
units.answer: 10. Index 1 selects the second row, and index 0 selects its first element.
units.complexity: One loop over n two-column rows takes O(n) time, with constant work per row.
units.mode: Core Kasa nested lists; no native table API.

units.title: Represent a record using a list
units.goal: Use a clearly documented field order to model simple structured information.
units.concept: We model a record as [name, quantity, unit price]. Every consumer must agree on the positions; Kasa core currently has no general dictionary or built-in typed record object. Real record schemas and field-name access remain separate experimental research.
units.source:
ma item = ["Akua", 12, 8]
ma total = item[1] * item[2]
ka item[0]
ka total
trace: Index 0 contains the name Akua; index 1 is quantity 12; index 2 is unit price 8.
Print the name and total. Changing positions without updating the program breaks the meaning.
units.task: Change the record to ["Kojo", 5, 9] and predict both output lines. Write down the three-field schema in plain language.
acceptance: Explains the intended meaning of all three positions.
Calculates the total from quantities rather than hardcoding it.
Distinguishes this list convention from a native typed record feature.
units.question: What happens if quantity and name positions are accidentally swapped?
units.answer: The positional contract is broken. Code may calculate incorrectly or produce a type error; core lists do not enforce named fields.
units.complexity: Fixed-position access and a single multiplication take O(1) time for this one record.
units.mode: Core Kasa list representation; typed records are not core builtins.

units.title: Validate values before using them
units.goal: Reject negative counts and count accepted versus rejected values before computing business metrics.
units.concept: Data processing must state its rules. Here, nonnegative numbers are accepted and negatives rejected. This is a domain check only: it is not a general-purpose type checker, schema validator, or untrusted-input security guarantee.
units.source:
ma scores = [10, -3, 20, 0, 15]
ma valid = 0
ma rejected = 0
ma i = 0
bere_a i < tentɛn(scores)
    sɛ scores[i] >= 0 a
        ma valid = valid + 1
    anyɛ_saa_a
        ma rejected = rejected + 1
    awiei
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
ka valid
ka rejected
trace: Start with five numeric scores and two counters at zero.
Count 10, 20, 0 and 15 as valid; treat -3 as rejected.
Print 4 valid and 1 rejected. Other validation rules would need to be specified separately.
units.task: Replace -3 with -1 and 0 with -2; predict the new counts. Explain why a negative score might be rejected, but a negative account balance may be valid.
acceptance: Counts accepted and rejected data correctly.
Documents the nonnegative-only rule and its limits.
Explains that this lesson does not validate data types or JSON structures.
units.question: Why is a validation rule not automatically suitable for every dataset?
units.answer: Different domains have different valid ranges. Negative quantities might be invalid, while negative temperature or balances can be legitimate.
units.complexity: A single pass over n values performs O(n) comparisons and uses O(1) additional counters.
units.mode: Core Kasa numeric range check; no typed validation builtin.

units.title: Calculate a total and average safely
units.goal: Aggregate numeric values and explain the empty-list division guard.
units.concept: A sum is built by visiting each item. Mean equals sum divided by count. This worked example uses a nonempty list; an independent solution should guard against an empty list before division. Kasa's numeric display may include .0 for a floating result.
units.source:
ma sales = [12, 18, 10, 20]
ma total = 0
ma i = 0
bere_a i < tentɛn(sales)
    ma total = total + sales[i]
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
ma average = total / tentɛn(sales)
ka total
ka average
trace: Count four observations, then divide 60 by 4 to get 15.0.
Print the total and average. Zero observations require a guard before division.
units.task: Replace sales with [2, 5, 8]. Predict the total and mean, then add an if guard for an empty list before dividing by its length.
acceptance: Calculates the correct total and mean for varying nonempty datasets.
Guards division when there are no observations.
Explains why these are descriptive summaries, not a full statistics package.
units.question: What should your program do when the input list is empty?
units.answer: It should handle the missing observations explicitly and avoid dividing by zero. A mean is not defined for zero observations.
units.complexity: One pass computes a sum in O(n) time and O(1) extra working space.
units.mode: Core Kasa list loops and arithmetic; no statistics package.

units.title: Filter and summarize stock levels
units.goal: Count positive stock entries and total their quantities in one pass.
units.concept: Filtering means keeping only values that satisfy a condition. This lesson counts strictly positive stock entries, ignoring zero quantities. It does not build a filtered list or provide a native query/table engine.
units.source:
ma quantities = [0, 4, 2, 0, 7]
ma nonzero = 0
ma total = 0
ma i = 0
bere_a i < tentɛn(quantities)
    sɛ quantities[i] > 0 a
        ma nonzero = nonzero + 1
        ma total = total + quantities[i]
    awiei
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
ka nonzero
ka total
trace: Start with five stock quantities and two summary counters.
Skip zeros, but count and add 4, 2 and 7.
Print 3 positive stock entries and a combined quantity of 13.
units.task: Replace the last quantity 7 with 0 and predict both totals. Explain why a negative value should be handled by a validation policy instead of silently treated as stock.
acceptance: Produces correct counts and sums for positive quantities.
Explains the exact filter condition and its consequences.
Does not misrepresent this as built-in CSV, JSON or table querying.
units.question: Does filtering a list automatically change the original values?
units.answer: No. This example only counts and totals matching values. It does not mutate the original list.
units.complexity: One pass over n quantities runs in O(n) time using O(1) additional counters.
units.mode: Core Kasa filtering with loops; tables/CSV/JSON not provided.
